name: Sultanates of the Malay world
summary: The Muslim port sultanates of the Malay world, such as Demak, Ternate, Tidore and Banten, that controlled the spice trade before Dutch dominance.

knownFor.label: Cloves of Ternate
knownFor.note: The Maluku islands were the only source of cloves.

knownFor.label: Great Mosque of Demak
knownFor.note: One of the oldest mosques in Java.

location.value: Port kingdoms across the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java’s north coast, the Moluccas (Spice Islands) and Borneo.
location.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

terrain.value: Coastal river mouths backed by rainforest and volcanic islands.
terrain.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

climate.value: Hot and wet all year; monsoon winds set the sailing seasons.
climate.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

resources.value: Cloves (Ternate, Tidore), nutmeg and mace (Banda), pepper (Banten, Aceh) and forest goods such as camphor.
resources.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

disasters.value: Volcanic eruptions and earthquakes in the Moluccas and Java.
disasters.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

population.value: Port cities such as Banten or Demak may have had tens of thousands of people; total numbers are unknown.
population.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

urbanisation.value: Life centred on walled or stockaded port towns where foreign merchants lived in their own quarters.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

disease.value: Malaria and smallpox; epidemics arrived with shipping.
disease.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

migration.value: Merchants from Gujarat, Persia, China and Arabia settled in the ports and spread Islam.
migration.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

economicBase.value: Taxing and organising the spice trade, which sold at huge profit in India, China and Europe.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

tradeRoutes.value: Malacca was the chief centre of trade in Indian cloth, Chinese porcelain and silk, and Malay spices; tin ingots served as a currency.

wealth.value: Rulers grew rich from customs duties and royal trade monopolies.
wealth.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

moneyAndTax.value: Chinese copper coins, local tin and gold coins, and Indian cloth used as currency; customs duties on ships.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

inequality.value: Sultans and nobles above free townspeople, debt-bondsmen and slaves.
inequality.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

governmentType.value: Sultanates where the ruler shared power with chiefs and a harbour master (shahbandar) who managed foreign traders.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

keyRulers.value: Sultan Baabullah of Ternate (expelled the Portuguese, 1575); Sultan Trenggana of Demak; Sultan Ageng of Banten.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

succession.value: Hereditary within royal families, often disputed.
succession.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

institutions.value: Islamic law alongside local customary law (adat); written law codes such as the Undang-Undang Melaka.
institutions.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

stability.value: Frequent rivalry between neighbouring ports, especially Ternate and Tidore.
stability.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

eliteConflict.value: Princes and chiefs competed for the throne and for trade profits.
eliteConflict.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

armyAndTech.value: Fleets of oared war galleys (kora-kora) and bronze cannon cast locally.
armyAndTech.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

majorWars.value: Wars against the Portuguese (from 1511) and then the Dutch East India Company (from 1600s).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

territoryChange.value: Taken over one by one by the Dutch East India Company (Banda 1621, Banten 1682).
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

alliancesRivals.value: Ternate against Tidore; temporary alliances with Portugal, Spain, the Dutch and the Ottomans (who sent Aceh guns).
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

inventions.value: No major inventions; skilled shipbuilding and navigation.
inventions.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

scienceEducation.value: Mosque schools and pesantren taught Islamic law, Arabic and Malay literature.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

openness.value: Very open to foreign merchants and ideas.
openness.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

communicationTransport.value: Ships of many sizes, from canoes to large junks.
communicationTransport.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

religion.value: Islam was firmly established under Muzaffar Shah (r. 1445–1459); whether Parameswara himself converted is unknown.

languageWriting.value: Malay was the trade language of the region, written in Jawi (Arabic script).
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

artsArchitecture.value: Mosques with tiered roofs (Demak Great Mosque) and court literature such as the Hikayat.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

socialStructure.value: Royal family, nobles, merchants, farmers and slaves.
socialStructure.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Malay-Islamic court culture across many states.
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

dailyLife.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

ideasReligions.value: Spread Islam through trade and Sufi teachers across the archipelago.
ideasReligions.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

colonisation.value: Portuguese took Malacca (1511); the Dutch East India Company controlled the spice islands by the late 1600s.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

riseSignals.value: Malacca Sultanate founded around 1400 (the conventional date) by Parameswara (Iskandar Shah), former king of Singapura; earlier dates have been proposed.

peakPeriod.value: Malacca’s height of glory was the mid to late 15th century; Mansur Shah (r. 1459–1477) expanded it greatly.

declineSignals.value: Dutch monopoly on spices, enforced by war (Banda massacre, 1621).
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia

outcome.value: Malacca fell to the Portuguese in 1511 (the successful assault was on 15 August 1511); Alauddin, son of Mahmud Shah, founded the Sultanate of Johor.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia.
sources.source: Wikipedia: Spread of Islam in Indonesia
